title: Economic Benefit
heading: Economic Benefit
sub: Density, yield loss and the conditional value of graded treatment.
description: Density, yield loss and the conditional value of graded treatment.

blocks.body:
The preceding models connect receptor recognition to color and paired colors to target density. When growers can already choose uniform treatment, what additional value does knowing the density provide?

Our economic model links density to potential yield loss, treatment costs and testing costs, then compares **net income over one production season**. The question develops from whether testing and control cover their costs to whether density information changes an action, and when that change is worthwhile.

The models have three consecutive roles. The [ODE](/model-ode/) describes color formation from receptor input and intracellular signaling. The **two-channel regression** uses paired color features to estimate Mi density despite a background contribution. Eco takes that density and compares outcomes using crop and management parameters.

**ODE pigment output → paired color features and regression → target-density estimate → economic scenarios.**

This example uses J2/100 cm³ soil. Paired readings require the same processing as calibration; density estimates enter Eco after checks on units and supported range. Economic parameters come independently from literature and scenario assumptions. Density connects color to income.

The simulated interface retains a point estimate and **regression prediction interval**. When the interval crosses a grading boundary, scenarios on either side show how treatment choice and income comparisons may change. Negative density, unsupported observations and estimates outside the economic model's domain cannot supply a valid report. Calibration-range handling must also be stated for each implementation. The current interval describes formal uncertainty in a simulated regression; coverage for real measurements remains to be tested.

blocks.text: From density to yield loss and income

blocks.body:
We use **protected tomato production in Spain** and *Meloidogyne incognita* as a specific example, with preplant density and income per hectare over one production season.

Relative yield follows the **Seinhorst relationship**, using the fitted spring-season result for ungrafted tomato from [Expósito et al. (2020)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2020.560024/full). Yield remains at its normal level below a tolerance density, then declines toward a lower bound. The converted tolerance is **6 J2/100 cm³** and minimum relative yield is **0.34**.
This equation is the implementation supplied with the example. Sales price, baseline production cost, treatment cost and avoided-loss fractions then determine net income:

$R_0$ is potential crop revenue; $e$ is the fraction of loss avoided by the selected treatment. Testing cost is included only for the test-guided scenario.

Economic and treatment inputs reference [Talavera-Rubia et al. (2022)](https://doi.org/10.3390/plants11202774). At a reference density of 100 J2/100 cm³, the reported population reduction is converted through the density–yield relationship into an **avoided-loss fraction**. That fraction is then held fixed across this example's densities. **Population reduction and avoided yield loss are different quantities**; this simplifying assumption affects the comparison.

The model combines yield and economic inputs from different studies into a reproducible literature scenario. Testing cost is provisionally **5 EUR/ha**, a **team assumption**. Prices, treatment costs and converted effects retain their sources for later local adjustment.

Comparing no testing/no control with test-guided treatment asks whether the combined detection-and-control program improves income, but includes the benefit of control itself. We therefore add **uniform treatment without testing** to examine the conditional value of density information.

| Strategy | Management rule | Testing cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No testing, no control | No dedicated nematode treatment | None |
| No testing, uniform control | The representative fluopyram program | None |
| Testing, graded treatment | Below 10: no dedicated control; 10 to below 80: middle treatment; 80 and above: high treatment | 5 EUR/ha |

The middle treatment matches the uniform-control program. The high treatment uses the chicken-manure biosolarization scenario. The boundaries **10 and 80 J2/100 cm³** are preset management bands, distinct from the yield tolerance at density 6. The model also compares available plans' income to check whether the preset choice matches the highest-income option under these parameters.

We keep two changes in income separate:

- **Improvement over no control:** the combined testing-and-graded-control program.
- **Improvement over uniform control:** the conditional value of adjusting action after obtaining density information.

This separates the value of undertaking control from the value of changing control because of new information.

At **100 J2/100 cm³**, with the example inputs unchanged:

| Management scenario | Net seasonal income (EUR/ha) |
| --- | ---: |
| No testing, no control | −1,828.19 |
| No testing, uniform control | 14,704.03 |
| Testing, graded treatment | 15,200.29 |

The graded program improves income by approximately **17,028.48 EUR/ha** over no control, but by **496.26 EUR/ha** over uniform control. The comparator changes the meaning of the benefit. In this scenario, additional loss avoided by stronger treatment covers the extra treatment and testing costs.

At low density, information may avoid unnecessary treatment. In the middle band, graded and uniform scenarios use the same treatment, so the difference is **−5 EUR/ha**, the added testing cost. At high density, stronger treatment is worthwhile only when the additional loss avoided covers its cost.

We separately varied testing cost, treatment cost, effect and crop price. When both strategies share a treatment, their common cost and effect parameters change together. These one-factor scenarios test sensitivity to assumptions. Real detection errors can select a treatment unsuitable for the actual density; evaluating that economic impact requires a measured error distribution.

blocks.text: Feeding economics back into detection design

blocks.body:
Semi-quantitative or quantitative results become useful when different densities imply different actions. Bias near an **action-changing boundary** can alter treatment selection, making these regions priorities for calibration and evaluation.

We therefore retain the density estimate, its management band and income against **both baselines**. Estimates crossing a boundary are accompanied by neighboring scenarios, exposing dependence on the density interpretation.

Future work will calibrate density estimates using real samples and phone readings, and update sampling coverage, testing cost per hectare and management inputs through application research. New data must test both discrimination near relevant boundaries and the cost of obtaining that information.

**Parameter configuration is separated from the calculation program**, with sample inputs and reproducible reports. Existing automated checks cover density–loss calculations, costs and baseline consistency; actual application benefits still need local evidence. Other teams can replace the crop, prices and treatments to evaluate their own management setting.

Move through the supplied economic scenario to see whether density changes the preset treatment and the comparison with uniform control. This browser version reproduces the density-to-income calculation from the submitted package. It takes density directly; it does not run the ODE or infer density from phone readings.
The model uses **deterministic scenario inputs**. Changes in income across densities are not income confidence intervals, and these Spain/tomato treatment bands are not universal agricultural thresholds. :::details[The supplied ODE–color–density prototype] The complete NemaKlear prototype also supports simulated mixtures and manual absorbance. Simulated mixtures run the two ODEs, show color development and pass blank-corrected endpoint absorbances to the two-channel regression. Manual readings enter the regression directly; accompanying ODE curves are explicitly references, rather than trajectories inferred from two endpoints. The prototype connects the estimate to management bands, potential loss, three-scenario income tables, income curves, interval endpoints and scenarios adjacent to crossed boundaries. It also provides reports and calculation downloads. The supplied prototype currently runs ODE r04 / two-channel r01, while the four research figures above use ODE r07 / two-channel r04. It requires a Python service and is retained as a local research package. The economic explorer on this page uses its supplied economic configuration without embedding that older density predictor. :::

1. [Expósito et al. (2020), source of the tomato density–yield relationship.](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2020.560024/full)
